questions.stem: Case 0001: The balance sheet of Birchfield Company lists an account named Accounts Receivable. Which element of the financial statements does this account belong to?

options.text: An equity item, because it represents owner investment
options.misconception: treats an operating claim as if it were a capital contribution

options.text: A revenue, because the sale has already been completed
options.misconception: confuses the asset created by a sale with the revenue earned

options.text: An asset, because it is a right to receive customer cash
A liability, because the customer still owes the company
options.misconception: mistakes a receivable from a customer for an amount the company owes

questions.explanation: Accounts Receivable is an asset: it is a present right to receive cash from a customer who was extended credit. The customer owes the company, not the reverse, so no liability exists. Revenue was recognized when the service was performed, but the receivable is the resulting claim to cash.
questions.hint: Ask who owes whom, then name the resulting claim.

questions.stem: Case 0002: Which of the following account types carries a normal debit balance for Birchfield Works?

options.text: Owner capital and revenues, which rise on the debit side
options.misconception: treats equity and revenue accounts as debit-balance accounts

options.text: Only cash, while all other assets carry credit balances
options.misconception: limits the debit normal balance rule to a single asset

options.text: Assets and expenses, which rise on the debit side
Liabilities and revenues, which rise on the debit side
options.misconception: reverses the normal balance of liabilities and revenues

questions.explanation: In double-entry bookkeeping, assets and expenses increase with debits and therefore carry normal debit balances. Liabilities, owner's equity, and revenues increase with credits and carry normal credit balances, so placing them on the debit side reverses their behavior. The debit rule applies to every asset, not just cash.
questions.hint: Remember that the accounts on the left side of the equation grow with debits.

questions.stem: Case 0003: On March 27, 2026, Cedar Supply pays $6,800 in cash to settle an outstanding supplier obligation. What is the effect on the accounting equation?

questions.stem: Case 0006: Which statement about a trial balance is correct for Pinecrest Services?

options.text: Equal debit and credit totals prove only that debits equal credits
A trial balance is prepared after the financial statements
options.misconception: reverses the order of the accounting cycle

options.text: A trial balance lists only asset and liability accounts
options.misconception: wrongly excludes revenue and expense accounts from the list

options.text: Equal totals prove that every transaction was recorded correctly
options.misconception: assumes a balanced trial balance guarantees error-free records

questions.explanation: A trial balance verifies the arithmetic equality of debit and credit balances, nothing more. Compensating errors, omitted transactions, or misclassified accounts can all leave totals equal. It is prepared before the statements and includes every ledger account with a balance.

questions.stem: Case 0007: On July 8, 2024, Willow Co. pays $5,400 of rent covering the current month. Which accounting principle justifies recording the full amount as this month's expense?

options.text: The business entity principle, which separates owner and firm
options.misconception: names the entity assumption instead of the period matching rule

options.text: The matching principle, which links costs to the period benefited
The revenue recognition principle, which governs sales timing
options.misconception: uses a revenue rule to justify an expense recognition

options.text: The cost principle, which records assets at historical cost
options.misconception: applies the historical cost rule to an expense timing question

questions.explanation: The matching principle requires expenses to be recognized in the same period as the benefits they help produce, so the $5,400 of rent for the current month is this month's expense. The cost principle addresses valuation, the entity principle addresses boundaries, and revenue recognition addresses sales, not costs.
questions.hint: Match the cost to the period that receives the benefit.

questions.subject: ACCOUNTING
questions.stem: Case 0008: Willow Manufacturing reports total assets of $7,650 and total liabilities of $2,600. What is total owner's equity?

options.misconception: subtracts assets from liabilities and reverses the equation
reports the liability figure as if it were the residual equity
adds liabilities to assets instead of subtracting them

questions.explanation: The accounting equation states that assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity, so equity is the residual $7,650 minus $2,600, which is $5,050. Adding the two sides double counts the financing of the assets, and subtracting assets from liabilities simply reverses the relationship.
questions.hint: Rearrange assets = liabilities + equity to isolate the residual.

questions.stem: Case 0009: Summit Group has total liabilities of $4,700 and owner's equity of $9,100. What amount of total assets must appear on its balance sheet?

options.misconception: reverses the subtraction of the two financing sources
uses only liabilities and ignores the equity claim entirely
subtracts equity from liabilities instead of adding them

Subtracting one financing source from the other would ignore that both claims fund the same assets.
questions.hint: Both creditors and owners have claims on the same assets.
